wolfram.note: N(2^1000000) with no explicit precision prints more significant digits (21) than a default/machine-precision computation can vouch for — Wolfram's own answer carries a `15.95...` precision annotation flagging the same limit. A real 'how many digits can we actually claim' policy question for default-precision N(), not a one-line fix.

our bug (emit): DEFINED_NAMES wrongly excluded m/s/q/A/C (and Integers had no CONSTANTS pass-through row) from free-variable treatment, so this row was reported un-emittable and skipped as unscanned. Fixed in reference/scripts/defined-names.ts's isDefinedName (a scalar-typed, non-constant lookupDefinition() hit is a free variable, same as no hit at all) and emit.ts's CONSTANTS (added Integers); now emits — leave for the next oracle scan to produce a real verdict.
An accuracy goal of 5 puts 5 digits after the point, 10 significant digits: 93648.04748. Wolfram prints 93648.0475, a digit short of the goal, though it keeps more internally.

1 - GoldenRatio + 1/GoldenRatio is exactly 0 (1/phi = phi-1), but N() returns a tiny nonzero residual (-2e-340) from catastrophic cancellation instead of recognizing the algebraic identity or padding with enough guard digits to show a clean zero, as Wolfram's `0``69.3` does. Needs either a GoldenRatio simplification identity or better cancellation handling in N(); same root cause as the row below.
An accuracy goal of -10 needs about 33 digits of E^100; we print 21, Wolfram prints more than it was asked for. The digits we print are all Wolfram's.
An accuracy goal of 20 on a number near 10^43 needs 64 significant digits, which we print; Wolfram prints the 60 its significance arithmetic vouches for. Its 60 digits are the first 60 of ours.
